books.section: Topic 4.9 The Development of an American Culture, B. European Romanticism and American Culture

stimulus.text: Thomas Cole's The Oxbow (View from Mount Holyoke, Northampton, Massachusetts, after a Thunderstorm), painted in 1836, looks down from a high, storm-darkened hillside. On the left, a gnarled tree leans over wild forest under black clouds. On the right, the Connecticut River bends through sunny, cleared farmland dotted with fields and small boats. A tiny figure with an easel stands on the rocks at lower right.
stimulus.source_note: Painting: Thomas Cole, The Oxbow, 1836 (Metropolitan Museum of Art). Public domain; image viewed before writing. Description records only what the painting visibly shows.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The contrast between the two halves of the painting most directly suggests which of the following?

options.text: Cole believed farming would destroy every American forest within a decade
options.misconception: The dark storm clouds look like a warning, so it is easy to read a fixed deadline into them.

options.text: The Connecticut River valley was still unsettled wilderness in 1836
options.misconception: The wild left half is so vivid that it is easy to miss the farms on the right.

options.text: American nature, both wild and being settled, held meaning for painters
European ruins were the best subject for American painters
options.misconception: European landscape painting used ruins, so it is easy to assume Cole wanted them too.

rationales.A: Cole shows farms already thriving on the right; he does not predict a date for the forests to vanish.
rationales.B: The sunny right half plainly shows cleared fields and boats, so the valley was already settled.
rationales.C: The painting holds wilderness and farmland side by side, and the storm light makes the meeting feel momentous.
rationales.D: America had no ancient ruins, so Cole painted wilderness instead; ruins were Europe's subject, not his.
rationales.general:
1. Read the painting in two halves. Left: storm, wild forest, a leaning tree. Right: sun, river, farms.
2. Ask what the split means. Cole is watching settlement arrive in the wilderness, and he paints the meeting itself.
Background from the books: Hudson River School painters prized wild nature and felt civilization closing in on it.
Remember: when a painting splits its scene in two, compare the halves before you decide what it means.

figures.caption: Thomas Cole, The Oxbow, 1836. Stormy wilderness at left, sunny farmland at right.
figures.alt: Thomas Cole's 1836 painting The Oxbow: a storm-darkened wooded hillside at left, the Connecticut River bending through sunny farmland at right, a tiny artist with an easel on the rocks below
